PSA vs PSC: Explain the difference betwe: Private Service Access (PSA) allocates an IP range from your VPC that's peered into the service producer's network (Google's, for services like Cloud SQL) - the managed service effectively gets an IP inside your VPC's address space, using VPC Network Peering under the hood; it's mainly used for Google-managed services that support PSA (Cloud SQL, Memorystore) and requires a dedicated allocated range plus a peering connection per VPC. Private Service Connect (PSC) instead publishes a service behind a single internal IP endpoint in the consumer's VPC without any peering or overlapping-range concerns, works for both Google APIs and third-party/your-own published services (via a PSC service attachment on the producer side), and scales better across many consumer VPCs since each just gets a simple endpoint rather than needing a full peering relationship - PSC is the more modern, flexible option and is generally preferred for new designs, especially when publishing your own services to other teams/VPCs.
StatefulSet: Basic Implementation. In th:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: frontend
  namespace: hacker-company
spec:
  serviceName: nginx
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      role: frontend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        role: frontend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
The StatefulSet's `spec.selector.matchLabels` and `spec.template.metadata.labels` must both be `role: frontend` to match the existing headless Service's selector - this is what lets the Service discover these StatefulSet Pods and gives each Pod (frontend-0, frontend-1) a predictable, individually addressable DNS name via the headless Service. `serviceName: nginx` links the StatefulSet to that specific governing Service by name, which is required for a StatefulSet to provide its stable network identities correctly.
Docker: HackerAPI Deployment, Environmen:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

docker run -d -i --name hackerapi \
  -e HACKERAPI_SECURITY_TOKEN="$HACKERAPI_SECURITY_TOKEN" \
  public.ecr.aws/docker/library/nginx:latest
`-d` runs the container detached (in the background); `-i` keeps STDIN open (interactive mode) without allocating a pseudo-TTY, which is what distinguishes it from `-it` (that combination would also attach a TTY); `-e HACKERAPI_SECURITY_TOKEN="$HACKERAPI_SECURITY_TOKEN"` reads the value from the existing shell/host environment variable of the same name and passes it into the container's environment - quoting the substitution protects against word-splitting if the token value ever contains spaces or special characters.
Dockerfile layer order: In a Go build st: COPY must happen before WORKDIR sets the active directory to /project, since WORKDIR only changes where subsequent instructions execute - it doesn't create or populate the directory's contents itself (though it will create the directory if it doesn't exist), so the source files need to already be copied in before WORKDIR is used as the location subsequent RUN commands operate from. Chaining `go mod download && go test ./... && go build` into a single RUN (rather than three separate RUN instructions) means all three commands must succeed for the layer to be considered valid - if `go build` were a separate RUN and the tests had already failed in a prior RUN, Docker's layer caching could still let you unknowingly build a broken/untested binary from a stale cached test-passing layer; chaining with `&&` ensures the build genuinely only happens after tests pass in that exact same execution, and using `&&` (short-circuiting on failure) makes the whole RUN - and thus the whole image build - fail immediately if any step fails.
Compose env var consistency: If a servic: Keeping both tied to the same `.env` variable guarantees the image tag you reference at runtime is exactly the version that was actually built with that build ARG - if they drift apart (e.g. the build ARG bumps to a new NGINX_VERSION but the image tag string doesn't update to match), you can end up building a new image correctly but then running a stale, differently-tagged image instead of the one you just built, or conversely tagging an image with a version label that doesn't reflect what was actually compiled into it. This mismatch is a classic source of 'works in build, not in the tag I'm actually running' confusion, and single-sourcing the version through one variable referenced in both places eliminates the possibility entirely.
Adding another Compose variant: To add a: Add a fourth service block following the same pattern as the existing three - its own `build.dockerfile` (or `BUILD_FILE`-equivalent argument) pointing to the variant-specific Dockerfile, its own `NGINX_VERSION` build ARG value (sourced from its own `.env` variable, distinct from the other three variants' versions), and an `image:` tag that incorporates that same variant-specific version variable so the tag and the build ARG stay tied together exactly as they are for the existing services - consistency here means literally mirroring the existing services' structure with variant-specific values substituted in, not introducing a different pattern for just the new one.
Describe a time when a production system: Use STAR: what specifically degraded and its user impact, how you detected it (an alert firing, a customer report - and whether detection was fast enough, which is itself worth reflecting on honestly), the immediate mitigation you took (rollback, scale, traffic shift) to restore service, and the concrete, specific prevention implemented afterward (a new alert, a validation gate, a capacity change) - specificity in each part, especially the prevention, is what makes this a credible and complete answer rather than a story that stops at 'and then it was fixed.'
Give an example of infrastructure you ar: Pick one concrete project and be explicit about the actual trade-off you weighed (e.g. choosing a simpler single-region design over multi-region for cost/complexity reasons, accepting slightly higher cost for better resilience) - naming a real trade-off you consciously made, including the downside you accepted, is far more credible than describing a solution with no downsides. Answering 'what would you do differently now' honestly (a genuine reflection, not a throwaway line) signals growth and self-awareness, which interviewers specifically listen for in this question.
Describe a situation where you had to cr: Describe the starting gap (no monitoring, or noisy/ineffective monitoring), the specific metrics chosen and why (tied to actual user impact, not just what was easy to measure), how thresholds were set (based on historical baseline data and business tolerance, not an arbitrary round number), and how you measured whether the change actually worked (reduced MTTR, fewer false-positive pages, faster incident detection) - the success measurement is the part that's easiest to skip but most important to include, since it proves the improvement was real rather than assumed.

Can you describe your professional backg: Structure in three parts under 90 seconds: a one-line professional summary (years of experience, core specialization), a brief walk through career progression highlighting only the roles/achievements most relevant to this specific role, and a closing line connecting your background to why this opportunity fits - tailor the emphasis to this role's actual requirements rather than reciting your full resume chronologically.
Walk us through a time when you improved: Structure as: the pipeline's state before (slow, flaky, or missing a key safeguard), the specific improvement made (parallelized stages, added caching, introduced a security gate, added canary deployment), a genuine challenge encountered during the change (resistance to a new required check, a tricky caching bug, a migration risk) and how you addressed it, and the measurable outcome (faster deploy time, fewer production incidents) - concrete specificity throughout, especially on the challenge faced, is what makes this credible.
How have you implemented observability a: Describe a concrete before/after - e.g. introducing SLO-based alerting where only threshold-based alerts existed before, or establishing a formal incident response process (severity levels, incident commander role, postmortems with tracked action items) where none existed - and tie it to a measurable reliability improvement (reduced MTTR, fewer repeat incidents, better on-call experience) rather than describing the practices in the abstract without a concrete outcome attached.
